lessons.title: Writing Prompts That Get Useful Answers
lessons.summary: Write prompts for AI chat tools that give the task, the context and the format you need. You will learn to turn a one-line request into a clear brief and to improve answers through follow-up instead of starting over.

sections.heading: Why vague prompts get vague answers
sections.body:
An AI chat tool does not know who you are, who will read the result or what "good" looks like for your task. When you type "Write an email to my manager", it has to guess the topic, the tone, the length and the outcome you want. The guess is usually bland and generic, and you end up rewriting most of it.

Think of a prompt as a brief you would give a capable new intern on their first day. The intern is quick and willing, but knows nothing about your office, your client or your deadline. The more of that missing information you supply, the less you have to fix later.

A useful test: if you handed your prompt to a colleague, could they do the task without asking you a single question? If not, add what they would have asked.

sections.heading: A simple structure: task, context, audience, format
sections.body:
Most good prompts answer four questions. Task: what exactly should be produced? Context: what background does the tool need? Audience: who will read or use the result? Format: how long, what structure, what tone?

Before: "Explain UPI."

After: "Explain how UPI payments work for a 5-minute talk to new joiners at a bank branch. Most of them are commerce graduates who use UPI daily but have never seen the back end. Give me 5 short bullet points in simple English, then one real-life example of a failed payment and what happens to the money."

The second prompt takes thirty seconds longer to write, but the answer is usable almost immediately. You do not need fancy wording or special tricks; plain, specific instructions work best.
do: State the task, context, audience and format
Mention the length or word limit you want
dont: Rely on one-line prompts for important work
Assume the tool knows your company or client

sections.heading: Show examples and set limits
sections.body:
If you want a particular style, show it. Paste a short sample of a past report or email you liked (with any confidential details removed) and say "Match the tone and length of this example." Examples often communicate more than a paragraph of description.

Constraints also help. "Under 120 words", "no jargon", "use Indian rupee figures", "avoid bullet points" or "give three options, not one" all narrow the answer towards what you need. You can also say what to leave out: "Do not include a greeting or sign-off; I will add those."

For tricky tasks, ask the tool to ask you questions first: "Before you draft, ask me up to five questions about anything you need to know." This surfaces gaps in your brief that you had not noticed.
do: Paste a short, cleaned-up sample of the style you want
Ask the tool to question you before drafting
dont: Paste confidential material as your example

sections.heading: Refine in conversation instead of starting over
sections.body:
The first answer is a draft, not a verdict. Instead of deleting the chat and retyping a new prompt, tell the tool what to change: "Make it shorter", "The tone is too formal; make it warmer", "Point 3 is wrong, our policy allows two weeks" or "Rewrite only the last paragraph." Specific feedback works far better than "Make it better."

When a prompt works well for a task you do often, such as a weekly sales summary or a meeting agenda, save it in a notes file. Next time, you only change the details. Over a few weeks you build a small personal library of prompts that saves real time.

Finally, remember that a well-written prompt improves the answer but does not make it correct. You still need to check facts, figures and tone before you use anything, which is the subject of the next lesson.
do: Give specific feedback on what to change
Save prompts that work for repeated tasks
dont: Say only "make it better"
Assume a good prompt guarantees a correct answer

takeaways: Write prompts like a brief for a capable new intern.
Cover the task, context, audience and format.
Show a short example and set clear limits.
Refine with specific feedback instead of starting over.
A good prompt improves the answer but you still need to check it.
quiz: Which prompt is most likely to give a usable first draft?
"Write an email to my manager."
"Write a really professional, polished and excellent email to my manager about the review that is impressive."
"Draft a 100-word email asking my manager to move Friday's review to Monday because the client data arrives Thursday night."
"Email. Manager. Review. Urgent."
It gives the task, the reason, the recipient and the length, so the tool has little to guess.
You want a summary in the same style as a report your team liked last quarter. What is the most effective step?
Describe the style in one word, such as "crisp"
Paste a short, cleaned-up extract and ask the tool to match its tone and length
Ask for the summary in any style first, then spend time fixing the tone, length and structure by hand
Type "Use the usual company style"
A concrete example shows the style better than a description, as long as confidential details are removed.
The AI's answer is good but too formal for a team WhatsApp update. What should you do next?
Reply: "Make this warmer and more casual, under 60 words"
Start a brand-new chat and type the original prompt again, adding the word "casual"
Reply: "Make it better"
Use the formal version anyway
Specific follow-up feedback refines the draft without losing the context already given.
Which detail is the "audience" part of a prompt?
"Use bullet points"
"Keep it under 200 words"
"Explain mutual fund NAV"
"For first-year B.Com students with no finance background"
Audience tells the tool who will read the output, which shapes vocabulary and depth.
You are unsure what information the tool needs to plan a team offsite agenda. What is a smart approach?
Keep regenerating until something looks right
Leave the prompt short so the tool can be creative
Ask the tool to ask you up to five questions before drafting
Copy a sample agenda from a website and ask the tool to reword it for your team
Letting the tool question you surfaces missing details before it drafts.
What is a reasonable test of whether your prompt is clear enough?
It is longer than three sentences
A colleague could do the task from it without asking you anything
It uses technical AI terms
It starts with "You are a world-class expert" and describes the tool's role in detail
If a person would need to ask questions, the tool is missing information too.
Which constraint would best help when asking for an explanation to put on a branch notice board?
"Make it detailed, comprehensive and cover every possible aspect of the topic"
"Use advanced terminology"
"Write as much as you can"
"Under 80 words, simple Hindi-English mix, no jargon"
A notice must be short and easy to read; the constraint matches the purpose.
You write the weekly sales summary every Monday. How can prompting save you time?
Save a prompt that works and change only the details each week
Write a brand-new prompt every week for variety
Ask the tool to remember all your sales figures permanently so it can write it alone
Skip checking the figures because the prompt is tested
A reusable prompt template saves effort, but the figures still need checking each time.
A colleague says, "If my prompt is perfect, the answer will be correct." What is the best response?
True, provided the prompt is long enough
True for numbers but not for text
Not quite — a good prompt improves the answer, but facts still need checking
True only for paid AI tools
Clear prompts reduce guesswork, but AI tools can still produce errors that you must verify.
Point 3 in the AI's draft states the wrong leave policy. What is the best follow-up?
"This is wrong."
"Point 3 is wrong: our policy allows two weeks' notice. Rewrite only point 3."
Delete the chat and start again
Ignore it for now and quietly correct it by hand later, in the final document before sending
Naming the exact error and the fix gets an accurate revision while keeping the rest.

scenarios.title: The generic presentation outline
scenarios.situation: Your team lead in Pune asks you to prepare a 10-minute talk on cyber-safety for branch staff. You type "Make a presentation on cyber security" into an AI chat tool and get twelve generic slides about firewalls and encryption. The talk is tomorrow.

options.text: Reply with a brief: "This is for branch staff, not IT. 10 minutes, 6 slides. Focus on phishing calls, fake KYC links and OTP fraud customers report. Simple language, one real-style example per slide."
options.feedback: It adds the audience, length, focus and format the tool was missing, so the next draft fits the real need.

options.text: Use the twelve slides as they are, since cyber security is cyber security.
options.feedback: Content aimed at IT teams will lose a branch audience and does not cover the risks they actually face.

options.text: Ask, "Make it simpler and shorter."
options.feedback: It moves in the right direction, but without the audience and focus the tool may simply shorten the wrong content.

options.text: Regenerate the answer several times until a better version appears.
options.feedback: Regenerating the same vague prompt usually produces variations of the same generic result.

scenarios.title: Using a past email as an example
scenarios.situation: You want the AI tool to draft a client update in the same style as an email your manager praised last month. That email contains the client's name, account details and transaction amounts.

options.text: Paste the full email so the tool sees exactly what worked.
options.feedback: Client names and account details should not go into an AI tool; the style can be shown without them.

options.text: Paste the email after replacing names, account details and amounts with placeholders like [Client] and [Amount], then ask the tool to match its tone and structure.
options.feedback: You keep the benefit of a real example while removing confidential information.

options.text: Describe the style in words: "short, polite, three paragraphs, ends with clear next steps."
options.feedback: A clear description is safe and helpful, but a cleaned-up example usually conveys tone more precisely.

scenarios.title: The draft that is almost right
scenarios.situation: The AI has drafted an internal announcement about new office timings. Most of it is good, but it says timings start "from next week" when they start on 1 December, and the closing line sounds too stiff.

options.text: Start a new chat and write the whole prompt again with more detail.
options.feedback: It can work, but you lose the parts that were already right; targeted feedback is quicker.

options.text: Reply: "Change the start date to 1 December and make the last line friendlier. Keep everything else the same."
options.feedback: Specific, targeted corrections fix the errors and preserve the good parts of the draft.

options.text: Reply: "Improve this."
options.feedback: The tool cannot tell what is wrong and may change the parts that were fine while leaving the wrong date.

cards.title: Prompts that get useful answers
cards.text: AI chat tools only know what you tell them. In two minutes, learn to write prompts that give you a usable first draft instead of a generic one.

cards.title: Brief it like a new intern
cards.text: Could a colleague do the task from your prompt without asking a single question? If not, add what they'd ask.
cards.good: Explain how UPI works for a 5-minute talk to new bank joiners. 5 simple bullets, plus one failed-payment example.

cards.title: Four parts of a good prompt
cards.text: Task: what to produce. Context: the background. Audience: who will read it. Format: length, structure, tone.
cards.example: Draft a 100-word email (task) asking to move Friday's review (context) for my manager (audience). Polite, no bullets (format).

cards.title: Set limits and show examples
cards.text: Constraints narrow the answer. A short sample shows style better than any description — just remove confidential details first.
cards.good: Under 120 words, no jargon, match the tone of the example below.

cards.title: Refine, don't restart
cards.text: The first answer is a draft. Tell the tool exactly what to change and what to keep.
cards.good: Point 3 is wrong — we allow two weeks. Rewrite only point 3.

cards.title: Before you press Enter
cards.text: Tap each one as you check it.
items: Task is specific
Background and audience are included
Length and format are stated
No confidential details in the prompt
cards.tip: Unsure what to include? Ask the tool to ask you five questions first.

cards.title: Build a prompt library
cards.text: Save prompts that work for weekly tasks, like sales summaries or agendas. Next time, change only the details. And remember: a great prompt still needs its answer checked.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Use these in your next prompt:

lessons.title: Checking AI Output Before You Use It
lessons.summary: Spot made-up facts, wrong figures and one-sided answers in AI output before they reach your manager or client. You will learn a practical way to verify claims and to match the depth of checking to the stakes.

sections.heading: Why AI can sound sure and still be wrong
sections.body:
AI chat tools generate text that is likely to fit your question. They are very good at sounding fluent and confident, but fluency is not the same as accuracy. A tool can produce a statistic, a quote, a book title, a court case or a web link that looks perfectly real and does not exist. This is often called a "hallucination".

Tools can also be out of date. Rules, tax slabs, company results and product details change, and a tool may describe an older version as if it were current. Arithmetic can slip too, especially in long calculations or when converting units such as lakh and crore.

None of this means AI is useless. It means the output is a draft from a fast but unreliable assistant. Once you use it, it becomes your work, and your name is on it.

sections.heading: Verify facts, figures and sources
sections.body:
Check every specific claim that matters: names, dates, numbers, quotes and rules. Go to the original source rather than another summary: the official website of a regulator or government department, a company's annual report, the actual policy document or the original study.

If the tool gives you links or references, open each one. Confirm the page exists and actually says what the tool claims. A real link to an unrelated page is as unhelpful as a fake one.

Recalculate any figure you will use. If the AI says sales grew from ₹42 lakh to ₹51 lakh, "an increase of 18%", work it out yourself in a spreadsheet: it is about 21%. Small errors like this are easy to miss and embarrassing when a client or manager spots them.
do: Check claims against the original source
Open every link and recalculate every figure
dont: Treat a confident tone as proof
Cite the AI tool itself as your source

sections.heading: Look for bias and missing views
sections.body:
AI tools learn from huge amounts of text written by people, so they can repeat the biases in that text. A job description drafted by AI may use language that subtly favours one gender. An answer about "typical customers" may assume everyone lives in a metro city, speaks English or has a salaried job.

Watch for answers that give only one side. If you ask "Why is remote work bad for productivity?", you will get arguments for that view, because the question assumed it. Ask neutrally instead, or follow up with "What are the strongest arguments against this?" and "Who might this advice not suit?"

Read the output as if you were the person it describes. If a customer, colleague or candidate would find it unfair or stereotyped, rewrite it.
do: Ask neutral questions and request counter-arguments
Read the text from the point of view of the people it describes
dont: Accept assumptions about gender, region or background

sections.heading: Match your checking to the stakes
sections.body:
Not every output needs the same level of checking. Brainstorming ten titles for a team newsletter needs a quick read for sense and tone. A client presentation, a report to senior management, anything involving money, health, law or a person's reputation needs every fact verified.

A useful rule: the more people who will rely on it, and the harder it is to take back, the more carefully you check. A message to a colleague can be corrected in a minute; a figure in a published report or a client email cannot.

Before you use AI output, ask one question: could I explain and defend every line of this if my manager asked? If the answer is no for any line, check it or remove it.
do: Check thoroughly when money, people or reputation are involved
Remove anything you cannot explain or defend
dont: Forward AI output you have not read in full

takeaways: Fluent and confident does not mean accurate.
Verify names, dates, figures and rules against original sources.
Open every link and recalculate every number you use.
Ask neutral questions and look for bias or missing views.
Check more deeply when the stakes are higher.
If you cannot defend a line, check it or cut it.
quiz: An AI tool gives you a statistic with a neat source link for your report. What should you do?
Use it, since a link is included
Open the link and confirm the page exists and contains that statistic
Ask the AI tool whether it is sure
Round the number slightly so that it looks less precise and harder to question
Links can be fake or point to pages that say something else; only the source itself confirms the figure.
The AI says revenue rose from ₹42 lakh to ₹51 lakh, "an 18% increase". What is the right response?
Trust it, since AI is good at maths
Change the wording to "about 20%" so the figure is roughly right either way
Remove the percentage and keep the rest unchecked
Recalculate it yourself; the increase is about 21%
AI arithmetic can slip; recalculating catches errors before others do.
Which is the best source to confirm a new rule announced by a regulator?
The regulator's official website or the original document
A second AI chat tool
A popular social media post about it
A forwarded WhatsApp message from a senior colleague who follows the news
Primary, official sources are the most reliable way to confirm rules.
You ask, "Why is hybrid work bad for teams?" and get only negatives. What does this show?
Hybrid work is clearly bad
The tool is broken
The question assumed one view; ask neutrally or request counter-arguments
You should ask in a different language
Leading questions get one-sided answers; neutral questions give a fuller picture.
An AI-drafted job advert says the ideal candidate is "a young, energetic guy". What should you do?
Keep it, since it sounds friendly
Rewrite it to describe the skills and duties, without age or gender
Change "guy" to "person" and keep "young"
Keep the wording but add "females may also apply" at the end of the advert
Job descriptions should focus on the role and avoid excluding people by age or gender.
Which task needs the most thorough checking of AI output?
Brainstorming names for an office cricket team
Suggesting icebreaker questions for a team lunch
Rewording your own out-of-office message before going on a week's leave
Figures in a presentation to a client about their portfolio
Client-facing figures involve money and trust and are hard to take back once shared.
What is a "hallucination" in AI output?
Confident, realistic-looking content that is false or made up
An answer that is too long
A deliberate lie that developers add to answers to test whether users are paying attention
Text written in an unusual style
The tool generates likely-sounding text, which can include invented facts, quotes or sources.
A colleague cites "AI said so" as the source in a team report. What is the best advice?
That is fine for internal reports
Add the name and version of the AI tool to make the claim more credible
Find and cite the original source, or remove the claim
Put the claim in a footnote instead
AI is not a source; claims need a verifiable original reference.
The AI describes a tax rule confidently, but you know tax rules changed this year. What is the main risk?
The tool may describe an older version as if it were current
The tool refuses to discuss tax
The answer will be too short
Tax rules are too complex to be explained in simple language by anyone
Tools can be out of date, so time-sensitive facts need checking against current official sources.
Which question is the best final check before using AI output at work?
"Does it sound impressive?"
"Could I explain and defend every line if asked?"
"Is it long enough?"
"Did the AI say it was confident?"
Once you use it, it is your work; you need to stand behind every line.

scenarios.title: The perfect quote
scenarios.situation: You are preparing a LinkedIn post for your company page in Mumbai. The AI draft includes an inspiring quote attributed to a famous Indian business leader. It fits perfectly, but you have never seen it before.

options.text: Search for the quote in reliable sources such as interviews or official speeches; if you cannot confirm it, remove it.
options.feedback: Made-up quotes are a common AI error, and a misattributed quote on a company page damages credibility.

options.text: Post it, since the leader is well known and the quote sounds like something they would say.
options.feedback: Sounding plausible is exactly how fabricated quotes slip through; public posts are hard to take back.

options.text: Keep the quote but remove the name, so it is not attributed to anyone.
options.feedback: It avoids misattribution, but the words may still come from someone else; it is better to verify or write your own line.

scenarios.title: Figures for the regional review
scenarios.situation: Your manager in Jaipur asks for a one-page summary of last quarter's branch performance by tomorrow. You paste the internal numbers into your company's approved AI tool and get a neat summary with growth percentages and a ranking of branches.

options.text: Send the summary as it is, because the tool used your own data.
options.feedback: Even with correct input, the tool can miscalculate percentages or mix up rows.

options.text: Check a few of the percentages; if those are right, assume the rest are too.
options.feedback: Spot checks are better than nothing, but for a management report every figure and the ranking should be verified.

options.text: Recalculate every percentage in a spreadsheet, check the ranking against the raw data, then send.
options.feedback: A report your manager will rely on deserves full verification; recalculating is quick and catches slips.

options.text: Ask the AI to double-check its own numbers and send whatever it confirms.
options.feedback: The tool may repeat or introduce errors; independent checking is what catches mistakes.

scenarios.title: The customer profile
scenarios.situation: You ask an AI tool to describe "the typical customer for a two-wheeler loan" for a training deck. The answer describes a young male office worker in a metro city.

options.text: Use it, since it is probably the most common profile.
options.feedback: It may reflect a stereotype rather than your data, and it ignores many real customers.

options.text: Check your company's actual customer data and ask the AI for a range of customer profiles, including women, small-town and self-employed customers.
options.feedback: Grounding the deck in real data and a range of profiles avoids bias and trains staff to serve everyone.

options.text: Ask the AI to rewrite it so the customer is a woman instead.
options.feedback: It challenges the default, but swapping one single profile for another still ignores the real range of customers.

cards.title: Check before you use it
cards.text: AI tools sound confident even when they are wrong. In two minutes, learn how to catch made-up facts, wrong figures and bias before they reach your manager.

cards.title: Fluent is not the same as true
cards.text: AI can invent statistics, quotes, court cases and links that look real. It can also describe old rules as current.
cards.example: Red flags: very precise numbers with no source, quotes you have never seen, links you haven't opened.

cards.title: Recalculate every figure
cards.text: AI maths can slip, especially with lakh and crore. Redo the sum in a spreadsheet.
cards.bad: ₹42 lakh to ₹51 lakh — an 18% rise. (Pasted straight in.)

cards.title: Go to the original source
cards.text: Open every link. Confirm facts on official websites, annual reports or the actual policy document.
cards.good: Source: company annual report, page checked

cards.title: Ask neutrally, spot the bias
cards.text: Leading questions get one-sided answers. AI can also repeat stereotypes about gender, region or background.
cards.bad: Why is hybrid work bad for teams?
cards.good: What are the pros and cons of hybrid work, and who does it suit?

cards.title: Before you use AI output
cards.text: Tap each one as you check it.
items: Names, dates and rules confirmed at the source
Every link opened and read
Every figure recalculated
No one-sided or stereotyped claims
cards.tip: Could you defend every line if your manager asked? If not, check it or cut it.

cards.title: Match checking to the stakes
cards.text: Newsletter title ideas need a quick read. Client figures, money, law or someone's reputation need every fact verified. The harder it is to take back, the more you check.

cards.text: Remember these before you hit Send:

lessons.title: Using AI Safely: Privacy, Confidentiality and Ethics
lessons.summary: Decide what you can and cannot share with AI tools and follow your organisation's rules. You will learn to remove personal and confidential data from prompts, and to be honest about when you have used AI.

sections.heading: Treat every prompt as sharing outside the company
sections.body:
When you type or paste something into an AI chat tool, it leaves your computer and goes to the tool provider's servers. Depending on the tool, your plan and your settings, conversations may be stored, reviewed or used to improve the service. Once it is sent, you cannot take it back.

The safest habit is simple: treat anything you put into a public AI tool as if you were emailing it to someone outside your organisation. If you would not send it to a stranger, do not paste it.

Many companies provide approved AI tools with stronger data protections under a business agreement. These are different from the free personal account on your phone. Know which one you are using before you paste anything.

sections.heading: What should never go into a public AI tool
sections.body:
Some information should stay out of public AI tools completely. Personal data: names linked to phone numbers, addresses, Aadhaar or PAN numbers, bank account details, health information or salary details. Confidential business information: unreleased financial results, pricing, client lists, deal terms, internal strategy, legal matters and HR cases. Security details: passwords, access codes and internal system information.

India's data protection law places duties on organisations that handle people's personal data, and your employer's contracts with clients usually promise confidentiality too. A careless paste can break both.

You can often still get help by removing the sensitive parts. Replace real details with placeholders: "Client A, a 45-year-old business owner in Nagpur" instead of a name and phone number; "[Amount]" instead of the real figure. The AI can help with the structure and wording without ever seeing the real data.
do: Replace names, numbers and IDs with placeholders
Use your company's approved tool for work data
dont: Paste Aadhaar, PAN, account numbers or passwords
Upload client files or internal reports to personal AI accounts

sections.heading: Know and follow your company's AI policy
sections.body:
Many organisations now have an AI policy that lists approved tools, what data may be used with them and which tasks need human review. Read it, and if your company has none, ask your manager or IT team before using AI for work data. No policy does not mean anything goes.

If you are unsure whether something is allowed, ask first. "Can I use the approved AI tool to summarise this vendor contract, or should legal review it directly?" is a sensible question, not a sign of weakness.

If you realise you have pasted something sensitive by mistake, tell your manager or IT team promptly. Early reporting lets them limit any damage; hiding it usually makes things worse.
do: Read your organisation's AI policy
Report accidental sharing quickly
dont: Assume a tool is approved because colleagues use it

sections.heading: Be honest about AI help
sections.body:
Using AI is not cheating in itself, but hiding it where honesty is expected can be. In colleges and many exams, rules say whether AI may be used for assignments; breaking them can count as academic misconduct. At work, some reports, client documents or published articles may need you to disclose AI assistance, or may not allow it at all.

AI text can also closely resemble existing writing, and AI-generated images may mimic other people's work. Check that your final work is genuinely your own wording and that you credit the sources of facts and ideas. Running AI output through a rewording tool to hide where it came from is still plagiarism.

Finally, you are responsible for how you use these tools. Never use AI to create fake reviews, impersonate real people, produce misleading images of someone, or pressure customers. If it would be wrong without AI, it is still wrong with AI.
do: Follow your college or employer's disclosure rules
Credit the real sources of facts and ideas
dont: Present AI work as entirely your own where rules require disclosure
Use AI to create fake reviews or impersonate people

takeaways: Treat a public AI tool like sending data outside the company.
Never paste personal data, client details, passwords or confidential results.
Use placeholders so AI can help without seeing real data.
Follow your company's AI policy and ask when unsure.
Report accidental sharing quickly.
Disclose AI help where rules expect it, and never use AI to deceive.
quiz: You want help wording a reply to a customer complaint. Which prompt is safest?
Paste the full complaint, including the customer's name, phone number and account number, so nothing is lost
Paste the complaint after replacing personal details with placeholders like [Customer] and [Account]
Paste only the customer's phone number so the AI can understand the context
Upload a screenshot of the customer's profile from the CRM
Placeholders let the AI help with wording without exposing personal data.
Which item is acceptable to put into a public AI chat tool?
Next quarter's unreleased financial results, to get help with the commentary
A colleague's salary details
A generic question about how to structure a project update email
Login details for the internal reporting system
General questions with no personal or confidential data carry little risk.
Your company has no written AI policy. What should you do before using AI with work data?
Use any tool, since nothing forbids it
Use only your personal account to keep it separate
Use any tool, but delete the chat history as soon as you finish
Ask your manager or IT team what is allowed
No policy does not mean anything goes; checking first protects you and the company.
You realise you pasted a client list into a personal AI account. What is the best action?
Tell your manager or IT team promptly so they can respond
Delete the chat and say nothing
Wait quietly to see whether anything goes wrong before telling anyone
Ask the AI tool to forget the data
Early reporting lets the organisation limit any harm; hiding it usually makes things worse.
Why is a company-approved AI tool often safer than a free personal account?
It always gives correct answers
It is usually covered by a business agreement with stronger data protections
It never stores any data at all
It means you no longer need to check the output because it is the company's own
Approved tools typically come with contractual protections, though output still needs checking.
Your college says AI must not be used for a graded essay. You used AI to write it and then reworded it with another tool. What is this?
Acceptable, since the words are now different from the AI's version
Acceptable if the essay is good
Fine as long as you cite the AI tool
Academic misconduct, because it breaks the stated rules
Disguising AI work where it is not allowed is still dishonest, whatever the wording.
Which use of AI is unethical regardless of the tool?
Drafting an agenda for a team meeting
Summarising a public news article
Writing fake five-star reviews for your branch
Translating a public notice into Hindi for customers at the branch
Fake reviews deceive customers; using AI does not make deception acceptable.
What is the most useful rule of thumb for a public AI tool?
Treat what you paste as if you were sending it outside the company
Anything is safe if you delete the chat
Personal data is fine if the tool is popular
Confidential data is fine in small amounts
Once sent, data cannot be pulled back; assume it has left your control.
A manager asks you to use AI to create an image showing a real customer endorsing your product. What should you do?
Create it, since the manager asked
Create it but make the image slightly blurry
Create it and post it without the customer's name
Decline politely and explain it would mislead people about a real person
Fabricating images of real people is deceptive and can harm them and the company.
Which detail should be replaced before asking AI to improve a loan rejection letter?
The general reason category, such as "insufficient documents"
The applicant's name, PAN and account number
The tone you want, such as "polite and clear"
The length limit of the letter
Personal identifiers are not needed for wording help and should be removed.

scenarios.title: The quick contract summary
scenarios.situation: Your manager forwards a 30-page vendor contract and asks for the key points by 5 pm. A colleague suggests pasting it into the free AI app on your phone. Your company has an approved AI tool, but you have not used it before.

options.text: Paste it into the free app, since it is faster and you will delete the chat afterwards.
options.feedback: Contract terms are confidential, and deleting the chat does not undo sharing them with an outside service.

options.text: Read and summarise the contract yourself without any AI help.
options.feedback: Safe and reliable, but slower than necessary if an approved tool is available for this kind of task.

options.text: Check the policy on using the approved tool for contracts, use it if allowed, and verify the summary against the key clauses.
options.feedback: It follows the policy, uses the safer tool and still checks the output before your manager relies on it.

scenarios.title: The awkward HR email
scenarios.situation: You are a team lead in Hyderabad. You need to write a sensitive email about a team member's repeated late arrivals and a personal health issue they have shared with you. You want help getting the tone right.

options.text: Ask the approved AI tool for a template: "Draft a supportive but clear email to a team member about repeated late arrivals, offering flexibility if there is a personal reason." Then add details yourself.
options.feedback: You get help with tone while keeping the person's name and health information completely out of the tool.

options.text: Paste the full situation, including the person's name and health details, so the AI understands the context.
options.feedback: Health information and HR matters are highly sensitive personal data and should never go into an AI tool.

options.text: Describe the situation with the name removed but mention the specific health condition.
options.feedback: Removing the name helps, but the health condition is still unnecessary detail; a general description would do.

scenarios.title: The internship report
scenarios.situation: You are finishing your summer internship report for your MBA college in Bengaluru. The college guidelines allow AI for grammar checking but require you to disclose any other AI use. You used AI to suggest the structure of two sections.

options.text: Say nothing, since structure suggestions are minor.
options.feedback: The guidelines require disclosure of AI use beyond grammar; skipping it breaks the rules even if the help was small.

options.text: Add a short note: "AI was used to suggest the outline of sections 3 and 4; all content and analysis are my own."
options.feedback: It follows the guidelines precisely and is honest about what help you received.

options.text: Rewrite the two sections from scratch without AI to avoid the question.
options.feedback: It avoids the issue, but it costs time unnecessarily; honest disclosure is all the rules ask for.

cards.title: Use AI without leaking data
cards.text: One careless paste can expose a client, a colleague or your company. In two minutes, learn what to keep out of AI tools and how to stay honest about using them.

cards.title: Every paste leaves your computer
cards.text: Prompts go to the provider's servers and may be stored. You can't take them back. Treat a public AI tool like emailing someone outside your company.

cards.title: Never paste these
cards.text: Tap each one to remember it.
items: Aadhaar, PAN, account numbers or phone numbers
Health, salary or HR details
Unreleased results, client lists or deal terms
Passwords and system access details

cards.title: Use placeholders instead
cards.text: AI can fix structure and wording without seeing real data.
cards.bad: Reply to Ramesh Kulkarni, 98xxxxxx21, account 4471…, about his failed EMI.
cards.good: Reply to [Customer] about a failed EMI on [Account]. Polite, under 100 words.

cards.title: Follow your company's AI policy
cards.text: Use approved tools for work data. No policy? Ask your manager or IT first. Pasted something by mistake? Report it quickly — hiding it makes things worse.

cards.title: Disclose AI help where expected
cards.text: Using AI isn't cheating. Hiding it where rules ask for disclosure is.
cards.bad: Rewording AI text with another tool so no one can tell.
cards.good: AI suggested the outline of sections 3 and 4; the analysis is my own.

cards.title: Wrong without AI? Still wrong
cards.text: Never use AI for fake reviews, impersonating real people or misleading images. You are responsible for how you use the tool.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Keep these rules in mind every time:

lessons.title: Using AI for Emails, Research and Summaries
lessons.summary: Use AI chat tools to draft emails, summarise long documents and start research faster, while keeping your own judgement in charge. You will learn practical prompts for each task and when doing it yourself is quicker.

sections.heading: Drafting emails in your own voice
sections.body:
AI is good at turning rough notes into a clean draft. Give it the key points, the recipient and the tone you want: "Draft a polite email to our vendor, Mr. Shetty, saying the delivery was two days late, asking for a revised schedule by Friday, and keeping the relationship friendly. Under 120 words."

Then edit the draft so it sounds like you. AI drafts often use long, overly polished phrases such as "I hope this email finds you in excellent health" or "I wanted to take a moment to reach out". Cut them. A short, direct email in your own words reads as more genuine.

Always check names, dates, amounts and promises before you send. The AI may add a commitment you never intended, such as "we will waive the charges", simply because it sounded helpful.
do: Give the key points, recipient and tone
Edit the draft into your own voice
dont: Send a draft containing promises you did not make
Keep flowery openings that add nothing

sections.heading: Summaries that are actually useful
sections.body:
A vague request like "Summarise this" gives a vague summary. Ask for what you will use: "From these meeting notes, list the decisions made, the action items with owner and deadline, and any open questions." For a long report: "Give me the five main findings in one line each, and any figures that affect our branch."

Only paste documents your company's policy allows, using an approved tool for internal material. Remove personal or client details if they are not needed for the summary.

Check the summary against the original before sharing it. Summaries can drop important conditions ("subject to approval" becomes "approved"), merge two people's tasks into one or invent action items that were never agreed. For anything you forward to others, skim the original sections the summary relies on.
do: Ask for decisions, actions, owners and deadlines
Compare key points with the original before sharing
dont: Paste documents your policy does not allow
Forward a summary you have not checked

sections.heading: Research: a starting point, not the answer
sections.body:
AI tools are useful at the start of research. They can explain unfamiliar jargon, outline the main aspects of a topic and suggest questions you had not thought of. If you are new to a project on electric vehicle financing, you might ask: "What are the key questions a lender should consider when financing electric two-wheelers in India?"

Treat the answer as a map, not the destination. Use it to decide what to look up, then go to reliable sources: official websites, industry reports, company filings and reputable news outlets. Note your sources as you go so you can cite them.

If the tool provides facts, figures or references, verify them before they enter your work. In a report, cite the original source, never the AI tool.
do: Use AI to explain jargon and suggest questions
Cite original sources in your work
dont: Treat AI answers as final research
Copy AI-provided figures without checking

sections.heading: Know when AI saves time and when it doesn't
sections.body:
AI tends to save time on first drafts, rewording, turning rough notes into a table, brainstorming options and drafting a translation into Hindi, Marathi or another language. A translation should still be checked by someone fluent before it goes to customers.

It saves less time, and can cause harm, on tasks that depend on judgement or relationships: final numbers, condolence messages, difficult feedback to a colleague, or a reply to an angry customer whose situation you know well. These deserve your own words, even if AI helps you think through structure.

A practical rule: if fixing the AI's draft takes longer than writing it yourself, write it yourself. Over a few weeks you will learn which of your tasks benefit and which do not.
do: Use AI for first drafts, reformatting and brainstorming
Have translations checked by a fluent speaker
dont: Outsource sensitive personal messages to AI

takeaways: Give AI the key points, recipient and tone, then edit into your own voice.
Check AI drafts for names, figures and promises you did not make.
Ask for summaries of decisions, actions, owners and deadlines.
Use AI to start research, then verify with original sources.
Write sensitive or judgement-heavy messages yourself.
quiz: Which summary request will be most useful after a project meeting?
"Summarise this."
"Make these notes shorter."
"Rewrite these notes in formal English."
"List the decisions, action items with owner and deadline, and open questions."
Asking for exactly what you will act on makes the summary immediately useful.
An AI-drafted reply to a customer includes "We will waive the late fee." You never decided that. What should you do?
Send it, since customers appreciate goodwill
Remove the line and check the rest for any other promises
Change it to "We may waive the late fee"
Ask the AI whether waiving the fee is allowed under company policy and follow its answer
AI may add commitments that sound helpful; only promises you can keep should be sent.
A summary says a budget was "approved". The original notes say "approved subject to finance review". What does this show?
Summaries can drop important conditions, so check them against the original
The meeting notes were wrong
AI summaries are always unreliable and should never be used for meetings or reports
The difference is too small to matter
Conditions often get lost in summaries; checking key points prevents misunderstandings.
You are new to a project on rural microfinance. What is the best way to use AI first?
Ask it to write the final research report
Ask it for statistics to quote in your presentation
Ask it to explain key terms and suggest questions to research further
Ask it to list sources and cite them in your report without opening them
AI is most reliable as a starting map; facts and sources need checking separately.
Which task is AI least suited to do for you?
Turning rough notes into a table
Brainstorming titles for a training session for new joiners at the regional office
Rewording a long paragraph more simply
Writing a condolence message to a colleague who lost a parent
Personal and sensitive messages need your own words and care.
AI translated a customer notice into Marathi. What should happen before it is displayed?
A fluent Marathi speaker should check it
Nothing; AI translations are always accurate
Translate it back to English with AI and compare
Display it with a small note saying that it was machine-translated
Translations can contain errors or awkward phrasing that only a fluent reader will catch.
An AI email draft opens with "I hope this email finds you in the pink of health and high spirits." What is the best edit?
Keep it, since it sounds polite
Make it even more formal so the vendor feels respected and valued
Replace it with a short greeting and get to the point
Move it to the end of the email
Short, direct openings sound more genuine and respect the reader's time.
You are writing a report and the AI gave you a useful market statistic. How should you cite it?
Cite the AI tool as the source
Find the original source, verify the figure and cite that
Use it without a citation
Write "according to recent research" without giving any further details
AI is not a source; only a verified original reference belongs in your report.
Fixing the AI's draft of a short team update is taking longer than writing it would. What should you do?
Keep prompting with more detail until the draft is perfect, however long it takes
Write it yourself and use AI where it truly saves time
Send the AI draft as it is
Ask a colleague to fix the AI draft
AI is a tool, not an obligation; use it only where it saves time.
You want to summarise an internal audit report. What should you check first?
Whether the report is long enough to need a summary
Which AI tool gives the shortest summary
Whether the AI tool will format it nicely
Whether your policy allows that document in an approved AI tool
Internal reports are often confidential; policy decides which tool, if any, may be used.

scenarios.title: Monday's inbox
scenarios.situation: You return from leave to 60 unread emails, including a long thread about a delayed project in your Chennai office. Your company allows its approved AI tool for internal emails.

options.text: Paste the thread into the approved tool and ask: "What was decided, what is pending, and is anything waiting on me?" Then read the latest emails yourself before replying.
options.feedback: A targeted summary saves time, and reading the latest messages confirms nothing important was missed.

options.text: Ask the AI to summarise it and reply to everyone based only on the summary.
options.feedback: Replying on an unchecked summary risks missing conditions or tasks assigned to you.

options.text: Read the whole thread from the start without AI.
options.feedback: Thorough and safe, but slower than necessary when an approved tool can help you get oriented first.

scenarios.title: The vendor delay email
scenarios.situation: A vendor in Surat delivered printed brochures three days late, and you need a revised schedule for the next order. You ask AI for a draft. It is polite but says "We will have to reconsider our partnership if this happens again" and begins with two lines of pleasantries.

options.text: Send the draft as it is; a firm warning will keep them on time.
options.feedback: You have not decided to threaten the partnership; sending it could damage a working relationship unnecessarily.

options.text: Remove the threat and the pleasantries, keep the request for a revised schedule by Friday, and check the dates before sending.
options.feedback: You keep the useful structure but make sure every statement reflects your actual position.

options.text: Soften the threat to "We hope this will not happen again" and send.
options.feedback: Better in tone, but the draft still needs the pleasantries trimmed and the dates checked.

scenarios.title: The research shortcut
scenarios.situation: Your manager asks for a one-page note on how UPI usage has grown in smaller towns. The AI gives a neat answer with three precise percentages and the name of a report, but no links.

options.text: Use the percentages and mention the report name, since it sounds official.
options.feedback: Precise figures and report names can be invented; unverified numbers in a note to your manager are risky.

options.text: Use the AI answer to decide what to look for, find the actual report or official data, and use only figures you can verify.
options.feedback: AI speeds up the start of research, while the note rests on figures you can source and defend.

options.text: Remove the percentages and keep the general points without sources.
options.feedback: It avoids wrong numbers, but a note without verified data is weaker than one built on real sources.

cards.title: AI for everyday tasks
cards.text: Emails, summaries and research eat up hours. In two minutes, learn prompts that speed these up — and when your own judgement must stay in charge.

cards.title: Give the key points
cards.text: Recipient, purpose, tone and length. Then edit it into your own voice.
cards.bad: Write an email to the vendor about the delay.
cards.good: Polite email to Mr. Shetty: delivery was two days late; ask for a revised schedule by Friday. Under 120 words.

cards.title: Watch for promises you didn't make
cards.text: AI may add commitments because they sound helpful. Cut flowery openings, too.
cards.example: “We will waive the late fee” — remove it unless you actually decided that.

cards.title: Ask for a summary you'll use
cards.text: Then check it against the original. Summaries can drop conditions or invent tasks.
cards.good: List decisions, action items with owner and deadline, and open questions.

cards.title: Research: map, not destination
cards.text: Use AI to explain jargon and suggest questions. Then verify facts in original sources.
cards.bad: Pasting AI statistics into a report, cited as “AI”.
cards.good: Using AI to plan what to look up, then citing the actual report.

cards.title: Before you send an AI draft
cards.text: Tap each one as you check it.
items: Names, dates and amounts are right
No promises you didn't decide on
It sounds like you, not a template
Translations checked by a fluent speaker

cards.title: Know when to write it yourself
cards.text: AI helps with drafts, tables and brainstorming. Condolences, tough feedback and final numbers need your own words. If fixing the draft takes longer than writing, just write it.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Try these on your next busy day:

lessons.title: Using AI Honestly in Your Job Search
lessons.summary: Use AI to tailor your resume, draft cover letters and practise interviews without inventing anything about yourself. You will learn where the line is during online tests and interviews so that a shortcut never costs you an offer.

sections.heading: Tailor your resume without inventing anything
sections.body:
AI can help you match your resume to a job description. Paste the job description and your resume (with your phone number, address and email removed) and ask: "Which skills in this job description are supported by my experience but missing from my resume? Suggest clearer bullet points using only the facts I have given."

The phrase "using only the facts I have given" matters. AI tools sometimes add skills, tools, certifications or results that sound impressive but are not true. Read every suggested line and ask: did I actually do this, and can I talk about it for two minutes in an interview?

Suppose Rahul, a B.Com graduate from Indore, interned at a CA firm. "Helped with GST work" can honestly become "Reconciled GST input credit for 15 small business clients over 8 weeks using Excel." That is stronger and true. Adding "Expert in financial modelling" when he has never built a model is not.

sections.heading: Cover letters and messages that still sound like you
sections.body:
Recruiters read many AI-written cover letters and quickly recognise the pattern: "I am thrilled to apply for this exciting opportunity at your esteemed organisation." Generic text tells them nothing about you.

Use AI for structure, then add what only you can provide: why this company or role, a specific experience that shows a relevant skill, and one detail that proves you have looked into the organisation. For example, mentioning that you volunteered at your college's financial literacy camp in villages near Nashik says more than three lines of enthusiasm.

The same applies to LinkedIn messages to alumni or recruiters. Keep them short, specific and in your own words. A three-line honest message often gets more replies than a polished paragraph that could have been sent to anyone.
do: Add a real reason and a specific experience
Keep messages short and personal
dont: Send a generic AI cover letter unchanged
Use phrases like "esteemed organisation" in every letter

sections.heading: Practise interviews with AI
sections.body:
AI makes a patient practice partner. Try: "Act as an interviewer for a bank probationary officer interview. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and then give feedback on clarity and structure." You can do the same for an HR round, a campus placement group discussion topic or a sales role.

Prepare answers from your real experiences: a college project, an internship, a part-time job or a responsibility at home. AI can help you organise them into a clear structure such as situation, task, action and result, but the story must be yours.

Do not memorise AI-written answers word for word; interviewers notice rehearsed scripts and ask follow-up questions. And if the tool gives you facts about banking, the economy or current affairs, verify them in reliable sources before repeating them in an interview.
do: Ask the AI to question you one at a time
Build answers from your own real experiences
dont: Memorise AI-written answers word for word
Repeat AI facts in interviews without checking

sections.heading: Where the line is: tests and interviews
sections.body:
Many selection steps are meant to measure your own ability: online aptitude tests, coding tests, written assignments, case studies and live or recorded video interviews. Using AI during these when it is not allowed is dishonest, and it can lead to disqualification or an offer being withdrawn later if discovered.

Read the instructions for every assessment. If they are unclear, ask the recruiter: "Is it acceptable to use AI tools for the take-home case study?" This is a reasonable question, and the answer protects you.

Remember that a job you get on false claims still has to be done by you. Background checks, probation reviews and your first manager will see your real skills soon enough. AI is best used to help you present the truth clearly, not to replace it.
do: Read each assessment's rules on AI use
Ask the recruiter if the rules are unclear
dont: Use AI during a test or interview where it is not allowed
Add skills or results you cannot back up

takeaways: Ask AI to improve your resume using only your real facts.
Reject any AI line you could not discuss in an interview.
Add a real reason and specific experience to every cover letter.
Practise interviews with AI, but tell your own stories.
Never use AI in tests or interviews unless clearly allowed.
quiz: AI suggests adding "Proficient in Python and SQL" to your resume, but you have only watched one tutorial. What should you do?
Keep it, since you can learn enough before the interview if you start tonight
Change it to "Expert in data tools"
Remove it, or write honestly that you are learning Python basics
Keep it but put it at the bottom
Claims must be true and defensible; honest wording about learning is acceptable.
Which prompt is best for tailoring your resume?
"Make my resume impressive for this job."
"Suggest clearer bullet points for this job description, using only the facts I have given."
"Add skills the recruiter wants to see."
"Write a resume for an ideal candidate for this role."
Limiting the AI to your facts prevents invented skills or results.
Before pasting your resume into a public AI tool, what should you remove?
Your phone number, address and email
Your internship details and the names of your supervisors
Your education section
Your list of skills
Contact details are not needed for wording help and are personal data.
A take-home case study's instructions do not mention AI. What is the best action?
Use AI freely, since it is not banned
Use AI only for the final draft and avoid mentioning it anywhere in your submission
Use AI and disclose it only if asked
Ask the recruiter whether AI tools are allowed
When rules are unclear, asking is the honest way to protect your candidacy.
Which cover letter line is most effective?
"I am thrilled to apply for this exciting opportunity at your esteemed organisation."
"I am a hardworking, dynamic and passionate individual."
"I would be grateful for a chance to prove myself."
"At my college's financial literacy camp, I explained savings accounts to 200 villagers in Marathi."
A specific real experience shows skills; generic enthusiasm does not.
How should you use AI to prepare for an HR interview?
Ask it to act as an interviewer, one question at a time, and give feedback on your answers
Memorise ten AI-written answers word for word
Ask it to write stories that sound more impressive than your own, and practise those instead
Skip practice, since AI answers are generic anyway
Interactive practice with feedback builds skill; your answers should come from real experience.
During a video interview, a friend suggests running an AI tool on a second screen to suggest answers. What is the risk?
None, if the interviewer does not notice
It is dishonest if not allowed and can lead to disqualification or a withdrawn offer
Only that the internet may be slow
It is allowed for technical roles
Assessments measure your own ability; secret AI use breaks trust and rules.
The AI-generated interview prep notes say a specific policy rate figure. What should you do before quoting it?
Quote it confidently, since interviewers like candidates who use numbers
Round it to sound approximate
Verify it from a reliable, current source
Avoid all current-affairs topics
AI facts may be outdated or wrong; checking protects your credibility.
"Helped with GST work" is your current internship bullet. Which AI suggestion is honest and stronger, if true?
"Led the firm's entire GST practice"
"Reconciled GST input credit for 15 small clients over 8 weeks using Excel"
"GST expert with in-depth knowledge of all direct and indirect tax laws across India"
"Saved clients crores in tax"
Specific, accurate detail strengthens a bullet; exaggeration can be exposed in an interview.
Why is inventing achievements a poor long-term strategy even if it gets you hired?
Resume software can always detect it
It is acceptable as long as you learn the missing skills quickly once you join the company
Recruiters never check resumes
Background checks, interviews and your actual work will reveal your real skills
False claims tend to surface quickly and can cost you the job and your reputation.

scenarios.title: The impressive extra skill
scenarios.situation: You are applying for an analyst role at a fintech in Gurugram. AI rewrote your resume and added "Built predictive models using machine learning". You did one college assignment using a ready-made template.

options.text: Change it to "Completed a college assignment applying a basic machine learning model to loan data" and prepare to explain what you learned.
options.feedback: It is accurate, still relevant to the role, and something you can confidently discuss.

options.text: Keep the line; everyone exaggerates a little.
options.feedback: An interviewer may ask you to explain the model, and the gap will be obvious.

options.text: Delete all mention of machine learning.
options.feedback: It removes the false claim, but you lose a small, true and relevant experience you could have described honestly.

scenarios.title: The online aptitude test
scenarios.situation: You are taking an unproctored online aptitude test for a graduate trainee role at a bank. The instructions say "Complete this test on your own without external help." A tough data-interpretation question appears with two minutes left.

options.text: Quickly paste the question into an AI tool on your phone.
options.feedback: It breaks the stated rules, and dishonesty discovered later can cost you the offer.

options.text: Make your best attempt, move on, and practise data-interpretation questions after the test.
options.feedback: You follow the rules, and your result reflects your real ability, which you can improve.

options.text: Skip the question entirely to save time for the rest.
options.feedback: Honest and sometimes tactically sensible, but an educated attempt may score if there is no negative marking.

scenarios.title: The AI cover letter
scenarios.situation: A friend shares an AI-written cover letter that "worked for him" at a bank in Kolkata. It is polished but generic. You are applying for a relationship manager trainee role at a different bank.

options.text: Use the same letter and change only the bank's name.
options.feedback: Generic letters are easy to spot and say nothing about why you suit this role.

options.text: Ask AI to rewrite the friend's letter in different words.
options.feedback: It avoids copying, but it is still generic; the letter needs your own reasons and experience.

options.text: Use AI for a structure, then add why this bank, a real customer-facing experience from your internship, and keep it under 250 words.
options.feedback: Your specific reasons and experience make the letter credible and memorable.

cards.title: AI in your job search
cards.text: AI can sharpen your resume and help you practise interviews. In two minutes, learn how to use it honestly — so a shortcut never costs you an offer.

cards.title: Stronger, but still true
cards.text: Ask AI to use “only the facts I have given”. Could you talk about each line for two minutes?
cards.bad: Expert in financial modelling (never built a model)
cards.good: Reconciled GST input credit for 15 small clients over 8 weeks using Excel

cards.title: Match the job description
cards.text: Paste the job description and your resume, without your phone, address or email.
cards.example: Which skills in this job description does my experience support but my resume doesn't show? Use only my facts.

cards.title: Make the cover letter yours
cards.text: Recruiters spot generic AI letters fast. Add a real reason and one specific experience.
cards.bad: I am thrilled to apply to your esteemed organisation.
cards.good: At my college's literacy camp, I explained savings accounts to 200 villagers in Marathi.

cards.title: Practise with an AI interviewer
cards.text: Answer with your own stories, not memorised scripts. Check any facts before repeating them.
cards.example: Act as an interviewer for a bank PO interview. One question at a time, then feedback on my answer.

cards.title: Stay on the right side
cards.text: Tap each one to agree.
items: No skills, tools or results I can't back up
No AI during tests or interviews unless allowed
If rules are unclear, I ask the recruiter
Facts from AI are checked before I use them

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Use AI to present the truth clearly:

lessons.title: AI for Finance Professionals: Client Data and Compliance
lessons.summary: Use AI to save time on drafting and preparation while keeping client data private and meeting conduct expectations. You will learn why suitability and advice stay your responsibility, how to check AI-generated figures and what records to keep.

sections.heading: Client data stays out of public AI tools
sections.body:
As a mutual fund distributor, investment adviser or bank relationship manager, you handle sensitive client information every day: PAN, Aadhaar, bank details, folio numbers, holdings, income, family details and goals. Clients share these because they trust you and your firm to keep them confidential, and regulators and employers expect the same.

Pasting this information into a public AI tool shares it with an outside service you do not control. Use only tools your firm has approved, and only in the way its policy allows. If you work independently, set yourself the same rule: no client-identifiable data in public tools.

You can still get help by anonymising. "Client A, 42, salaried, moderate risk profile, goal: child's education in 10 years" lets an AI help you structure an explanation without any real identity. Never include names, phone numbers, PAN, account or folio numbers, or screenshots of statements.
do: Use only firm-approved tools for client work
Anonymise client situations before asking for help
dont: Paste PAN, folio numbers or statements into public tools
Upload client screenshots to personal AI accounts

sections.heading: Suitability and advice remain your responsibility
sections.body:
An AI tool does not know your client's full financial situation, risk appetite, existing commitments or the conversations you have had. It is not registered with any regulator and is not accountable for the outcome. Whatever you recommend to a client is your recommendation, even if an AI suggested it.

So never forward an AI-generated product list or portfolio to a client as advice. Suitability comes first: understand the client's goals, time horizon and risk profile, then consider options within the scope your registration and role allow. A distributor, for example, should not drift into the kind of personalised advice that requires a different registration.

AI can still help with preparation: drafting a list of questions to ask in a review meeting, explaining a concept in plain language, or creating a checklist for documents a client needs. Use it to support your process, not to replace your judgement.
do: Base every recommendation on your own suitability assessment
Use AI to prepare questions and plain-language explanations
dont: Forward AI fund suggestions to clients as advice
Let AI push you beyond the scope of your registration

sections.heading: Check every number, rule and claim
sections.body:
AI tools can state fund returns, expense ratios, exit loads, tax treatment or regulatory rules incorrectly or out of date. These details change, and a confident wrong figure in a client conversation can mislead the client and expose you.

Verify against primary sources: the scheme information document and the latest factsheet from the fund house, official industry and regulator websites, and current tax rules from official sources. For any calculation, such as an SIP projection, redo it yourself and make clear that projections are illustrations, not promises.

Watch the language too. AI drafts may include phrases such as "safe returns", "guaranteed growth" or "best fund". Market-linked products cannot promise returns, and communications must be fair, balanced and include the required risk disclosures. Any client-facing material, such as a newsletter or social media post, should go through your firm's compliance review where one exists.
do: Check figures against factsheets and official sources
Send client-facing content for compliance review
dont: Use phrases like "guaranteed returns" or "safe" for market-linked products
Share AI-calculated projections without rechecking

sections.heading: Keep records and stay transparent
sections.body:
Good record-keeping protects both you and your client. Keep the final version of what you actually communicated, the reasons behind a recommendation and the client's documented risk profile, as your firm and applicable rules require. If AI helped draft a message, the record is the version you sent, and you are responsible for it.

Transparency applies with or without AI. Disclose your commission or fees as required, explain risks in plain language and never use AI to write pressure scripts that rush a client into a decision. A message such as "Only two days left to lock in this return!" is mis-selling, whoever wrote it.

Used well, AI can make you more efficient: preparing meeting agendas, drafting educational explainers on topics like asset allocation, or summarising a public regulatory update before you read the original. The principle is simple: AI can help you work faster, but the client's interest, the rules and the final judgement stay with you.
do: Keep the final sent version and reasons for recommendations
Disclose fees or commission clearly
dont: Use AI to write urgency or pressure messages
Rely on an AI summary of a regulatory update without reading the original

takeaways: Keep client-identifiable data out of public AI tools; anonymise instead.
Suitability and recommendations are your responsibility, not the AI's.
Verify every figure, rule and projection against official sources.
Never promise returns; send client content for compliance review.
Keep records of what you sent and why, and disclose fees clearly.
quiz: You want help explaining asset allocation to a client. Which prompt is acceptable in a public AI tool?
"Client Sunita Rao, PAN ABCDE1234F, holds these funds — explain allocation to her."
"Explain asset allocation simply for a 42-year-old salaried client with a moderate risk profile."
Upload her latest consolidated account statement and ask the tool for a simple explanation of her mix
Paste her folio numbers so the AI can see her holdings
An anonymised description gets useful help without exposing client data.
An AI tool lists "the top five funds" for a client's goal. What should you do?
Forward the list to the client as your recommendation
Forward it with a note explaining that an AI tool chose them, so the client knows
Ignore AI completely for all client work
Use your own suitability assessment; the AI's list is not advice
Recommendations must come from your assessment of the client's needs, within your role.
An AI draft newsletter says "This fund offers safe, guaranteed growth." What is the main problem?
Market-linked products cannot promise returns, so the claim is misleading
The newsletter is too short
It should compare more funds and name the top performers of the last five years
Clients prefer longer explanations
Promising returns on market-linked products is misleading and against conduct expectations.
Where should you verify a fund's current expense ratio before telling a client?
Ask the AI tool again
A popular finance influencer's video explaining the fund's costs
The fund house's latest factsheet or official disclosures
A colleague's memory of last year's figure
Official, current documents are the reliable source for scheme details.
AI calculated an SIP projection for a client presentation. What is the right approach?
Use it as is, since the AI is good at maths
Recalculate it yourself and present it as an illustration, not a promise
Round it up to make it more attractive
Remove the assumptions from the slide so it looks cleaner and easier to read
Projections need checking and clear framing as illustrations based on assumptions.
You are a mutual fund distributor. An AI tool helps you build a detailed personalised plan that goes beyond distribution. What is the concern?
The plan may be too long
AI-generated plans are always wrong and clients can easily tell
Clients do not like written plans
It may take you beyond the scope your registration allows
Stay within your role; AI does not change what your registration permits.
Which use of AI is appropriate for a relationship manager?
Drafting a list of questions to ask a client in an annual review
Writing "Last chance — offer closes tonight!" messages to clients
Pasting a client's bank statement into a public tool to analyse spending
Generating a recommendation to send without review
Preparing questions supports your process without exposing data or replacing judgement.
AI summarised a new regulatory update for you. What should you do before acting on it?
Share the summary with clients immediately
Assume it is accurate if it sounds formal
Read the original update or your firm's compliance note
Ask a second AI tool to confirm it, and act on it if both agree
AI summaries can miss or misstate details; the original or compliance guidance is authoritative.
If AI helped draft a client email, what should your records contain?
Nothing, since AI wrote it
The final version you sent and the reasons for any recommendation
Only the AI prompt
Only the client's reply
You are responsible for what you sent; keep it as your firm's rules require.
A client asks whether you use AI. What is the best answer?
Deny it to avoid worrying them
Say AI makes all your decisions now
Change the subject to fund performance
Explain honestly that you may use approved tools for drafting, but recommendations are your own and their data stays private
Honest transparency builds trust and makes your responsibility clear.

scenarios.title: The portfolio review shortcut
scenarios.situation: You are an RM at a bank branch in Lucknow with eight client reviews this week. A colleague suggests uploading each client's consolidated statement to a free AI app to "get a quick analysis". Your bank has an approved internal AI tool, but its policy does not cover client statements.

options.text: Upload the statements to the free app, but blur the names first.
options.feedback: Statements contain many identifiers beyond names, and the free app is not approved for client data.

options.text: Use the approved tool to prepare a general review checklist and question list, and analyse each portfolio yourself using the bank's systems.
options.feedback: You save time on preparation while keeping client data within approved systems and your judgement in charge.

options.text: Do all eight reviews manually without any AI.
options.feedback: Safe and compliant, but you miss easy time savings on preparation that policy allows.

options.text: Upload the statements to the approved internal tool, since it is the bank's own.
options.feedback: The policy does not cover client statements; check with compliance before using any tool for that data.

scenarios.title: The festive campaign post
scenarios.situation: Before Diwali, you ask AI to write a social media post for your mutual fund distribution business in Ahmedabad. The draft says: "Light up your wealth this Diwali! Our top fund delivered 25% last year — start an SIP today for assured growth."

options.text: Post it, since the 25% figure is real.
options.feedback: Highlighting one year's return and promising "assured growth" is misleading for market-linked products.

options.text: Remove "assured growth" and the return figure, and post it.
options.feedback: It removes the worst problems, but the post still needs the required risk disclosure and any applicable review.

options.text: Rewrite it as an educational post about starting an SIP for long-term goals, add the required risk disclosure, and get it reviewed as your firm or rules require.
options.feedback: Educational, balanced content with proper disclosure meets conduct expectations and still uses the festive moment.

scenarios.title: The client who asked AI
scenarios.situation: A 58-year-old client in Kochi tells you an AI chat tool recommended moving most of her retirement savings into a sectoral equity fund. She wants you to process the switch today.

options.text: Process the switch, since it is her decision.
options.feedback: Processing without discussing suitability ignores your duty to act in the client's interest.

options.text: Tell her AI tools are useless and she should ignore them.
options.feedback: Your caution is right, but dismissing her research can feel condescending; explaining the reasons helps her decide.

options.text: Review her goals, time horizon and risk profile with her, explain the concentration risk of a sectoral fund near retirement, and document the discussion and her final decision.
options.feedback: You respect her choice while applying suitability, explaining the risks clearly and keeping a record.

cards.title: AI with client data
cards.text: AI can save you hours on prep and drafting. In two minutes, learn how to use it without exposing client data or crossing compliance lines.

cards.title: Anonymise every client situation
cards.text: Use only firm-approved tools. No names, PAN, folio numbers or statements in public AI tools.
cards.bad: Sunita Rao, PAN ABCDE1234F, holds these funds…
cards.good: Client A, 42, salaried, moderate risk, goal: child's education in 10 years.

cards.title: Suitability is your job
cards.text: AI doesn't know your client and isn't accountable. Stay within what your registration allows.
cards.bad: Forwarding an AI “top five funds” list to a client.
cards.good: Using AI to prepare review questions, then recommending from your own assessment.

cards.title: Verify every figure and rule
cards.text: Returns, expense ratios, exit loads and tax rules change. Check factsheets and official sources. Recalculate projections and call them illustrations, not promises.

cards.title: Remove promises from AI drafts
cards.text: Market-linked products can't promise returns. Add risk disclosures and get compliance review.
cards.bad: Start an SIP today for assured growth!
cards.good: SIPs can help you invest regularly for long-term goals. Returns are market-linked.

cards.title: Before anything reaches a client
cards.text: Tap each one as you check it.
items: No client data went into a public tool
Figures checked against official sources
No promised returns or pressure lines
Fees or commission disclosed
Final version and reasons saved
